title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
summary:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.

title: Vercel Security Review no longer requires a linked Vercel project
summary:
You can now scan code changes for vulnerabilities with Vercel Security Review in GitHub repositories that have not yet been linked to a Vercel project.

By default, Security Review covers all unlinked repositories the Vercel GitHub App can access in a connected GitHub account. You can limit coverage to selected connected accounts or individual repositories in Agent settings. Once enabled, each push to a covered repository automatically triggers a review of its code changes.

Security Review checks commits directly in repositories with Security Review enabled, without requiring a Vercel project or deployment. When a push creates a deployment for a linked project with Security Review enabled, the review uses the additional project and deployment context.

Connect the account in your team’s Git settings, then enable Security Review in Vercel Agent settings.

Get started with the Security Review documentation.

title: Vercel Sandbox starts up to 4x faster
summary:
Vercel Sandbox now initializes up to 4x faster outside the Washington, D.C. (iad1) region when reused image data is served from a regional cache.

Initialization now reads cached image data close to where the sandbox runs, avoiding round trips to origin image storage in iad1 on cache hits. Regional caching supports managed and custom images backed by Vercel Container Registry, including snapshots based on those images.

In internal end-to-end benchmarks with Vercel Managed Images, startup time fell about 75% in Paris and from about 3.5s to 1.05s in Seoul. Regions closer to origin storage generally see smaller improvements because requests already travel a shorter distance.

Learn more in the Vercel Sandbox documentation.

title: Build cache size limit on Vercel increased to 5 GB
summary:
The build cache size limit on all Vercel build machines has been increased to 5 GB. This allows projects to save more installed dependencies and framework files for reuse between deployments, which can reduce install and build times.

Build machines are the compute environments that install dependencies and build your project before deployment. Previously, caches were discarded if they exceeded 1.5 GB on Basic and Standard, 3 GB on Enhanced, or 4.75 GB on Turbo, leaving the next build without a cache.

The change applies automatically across all build machine types at no additional charge, with no configuration required.

Learn more in the build cache documentation.

title: Parallel Decisions now available on AI Gateway for free
summary:
Parallel Decisions Fast from Parallel is now available on AI Gateway and is free through November 23, 2026.

It searches the live web to answer typed questions about companies, products, policies, and other changing information, returning probabilities and cited evidence for your application to act on.

Use it to enrich CRM records, check eligibility, route leads, or verify claims against current sources. Boolean questions return the probability of yes, Choice questions select from options you define, and Score questions assess an ordered rubric. Related questions share context and retrieved evidence in one request.

Use parallel/parallel-decisions-fast as the model name. No separate Parallel account is required. These examples ask the same web-grounded question through the AI SDK, TypeSafe-compatible API, and OpenAI-compatible Decisions API.

Citations include source URLs, optional titles, and evidence excerpts. They apply to the whole request, rather than mapping individual sources to each answer. Your application can use answer probabilities to act automatically above a threshold and send uncertain results for review.

AI Gateway tracks these requests in logs and spend budgets alongside other model requests. Read the decision model documentation for question types, or browse the model catalog.

title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
summary:
When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits.

Last year, we shipped just that, with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it.

More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged.

  • The first is automation: Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines.

  • The second is agents and harnesses: Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too.

As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance.

Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three.

More secure workflows

The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection.

Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end, before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools.

Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel

On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change:

Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log.

Encryption on self-hosted Worlds

Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams.

A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management. Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay:

More security work in v5

Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads.

You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0, inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability.

A redesigned trace viewer

The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development.

Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets.

Workflows in every region

In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1. Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress.

For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region. Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path.

By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration:

To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start(). That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay:

The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1.

Infrastructure reliability

Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover.

With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors.

As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug.

Agent-ready performance

In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today.

Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit.

In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes.

The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures.

Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers:

Fewer queue hops

In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout.

The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms.

Incremental replay

Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log: replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms. The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes.

WebSocket streaming

Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default. In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds.

Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression.

These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application.

Worlds: the shared durability primitive

Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World: the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness, which adds durability to existing agent harnesses.

Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness.

Choose the integration around how you want to build:

  • Workflow SDK: write durable application logic with use workflow and use step.

  • WorkflowAgent: use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow.

  • fx: embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx.

  • durable-harness: keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it.

    • Supports Pi and OpenCode, with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox.

  • eve: build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds.

We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability.

Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds:

  • In-flight cancellation with AbortController

  • Searchable run attributes

  • More framework integrations

  • And more

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports managed npm credentials
summary:

summary:

title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
summary:
AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August, September, and October.

November 2026 Summary

  • In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model.

  • About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July.

  • OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one. OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December.

  • More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on.

Decision models account for 26% of all requests

Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive.

Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model.

They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model.

Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend.

Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models.

Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did.

This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively.

Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July

About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%.

New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%.

Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July.

A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps:

  • A voice model turns the user’s speech into text

  • A language model writes the reply

  • Another voice model reads the reply back to the user

Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled.

Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped.

For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both.

Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds

Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54.

Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five.

Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI.

But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

Read more about our methodology, and explore or download the public data.

On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period.

Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old

Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten.

Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models.

Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab.

Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens.

AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one.

Also in October’s data

  • Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two.

  • Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten.

  • OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0.

About this data

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ.

  • Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month.

  • Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list.

  • Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025.

  • Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens.

  • Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day.

  • A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month.

  • All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Workflow SDK now writes over WebSockets on Vercel
summary:
The Workflow SDK now sends event writes and stream writes to Vercel Workflows over a WebSocket by default, replacing one HTTP request per write, or per write group for streams. No code change is needed beyond upgrading to workflow@5.2.0 or later.

Once you deploy the upgrade, new runs use it. In-flight runs finish on the deployment they started on.

Existing streaming code works as is. A step that writes a burst of chunks, like AI tokens, sends them over the WebSocket once it opens:

In a benchmark replaying an AI agent's token stream, v5.2.0, which writes streams over a WebSocket by default, delivered the full response 4.2× faster than v4.8.12, with no chunk delayed over a second.

Every step start and completion is an event write, now sent over the WebSocket, so workflows with many steps make fewer HTTP requests. The added efficiency also improves performance and reduces costs. The queue handler opens the connection for every delivery.

title: Vercel Container Registry now supports 2 GB compressed image layers
summary:
Vercel Container Registry now supports compressed image layers of up to 2 GB each, up from 500 MB, the total image size limit stays 15 GB.

The registry works with standard workflows like docker push, docker pull, and docker tag, and pushing an image creates the repository on the fly.

If background optimization of a pushed image fails, the image shows an error status in the dashboard, and pushing the same image again retries the conversion.

title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render
summary:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available
summary:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect , and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

title: Token Pass credit now applies automatically across AI Gateway
summary:
Token Pass credit now applies automatically to included model usage through AI Gateway, whether a request authenticates with an API key, OIDC token, or fx login. No dedicated Token Pass API key is required, though you can still create one from the dashboard or the CLI for keys scoped only to featured models and providers.

When Token Pass credit runs out for the billing period, requests from a standard key or OIDC token fall back to your team's AI Gateway credits. Token Pass keys still stop until the next billing period.

Requests served through the Token Pass provider remain Zero Data Retention (ZDR). Fallback requests follow your team's setting. With team-wide ZDR enabled, they route only to ZDR providers.

Available now for Token Pass subscribers on Pro teams. If you created a Token Pass key during setup, switch to a standard API key or OIDC token to get fallback. Learn more in the Token Pass documentation.
